newsitem.title: CHINA: HK says labour laws frozen to allow time for review.
newsitem.headline: HK says labour laws frozen to allow time for review.

text.p: Hong Kong's new government on Thursday defended a controversial rollback of labour rights laws, saying they had been passed with "indecent haste" in the last days of British rule and needed careful review.
"From the government's point of view, we asked for these bills to be suspended to give us time to look at them," commissioner for labour Jacqueline Willis told reporters.
"Does this mean that we're turning back the clock? I can assure you we are not doing that."
Last week, the unelected Provisional Legislature endorsed a bill freezing until October laws on collective bargaining, use of trade union funds and anti-union discrimination by employers.

The move, ostensibly on the grounds that the three laws may hurt Hong Kong's competitiveness, sparked an uproar among local pro-democracy unions and labour groups world wide, who bombarded the territory's leader Tung Chee-hwa with letters of protest.
One of the most contentious issues within the frozen laws is the obligation on employers to join in collective bargaining with unions.
Citing Hong Kong's role as a free-market haven, Willis said her department has not seen the need to make collective bargaining anything other than voluntary.
"Mandatory collective bargaining is a major departure from policy," she said.

Willis said the Labour Department was concerned about the content of the bills even before they were passed into law by the Legislative Council, which ceased to exist when Britain handed back Hong Kong to China on July 1.

"Our concerns about these pieces of legislation before the handover and after the handover are still there," she said. "We needed time, and the advice we gave to the member sponsoring the bill was 'Don't proceed with this'."
Despite the request, the bills were passed by the now defunct elected chamber with "indecent haste", Willis said.
The new laws created financial and policy problems for the people administering them, she added.
"We respect legislative process, but in the process if the law is defective, should we turn a blind eye?"

The Labour Advisory Board -- which groups representatives from business, unions and the government -- met this week to study the three laws, but reached no conclusion and sent the problem to a labour relations panel for further study.
